Skip to content. toolbar 1 Geometry and Functions Intended Learning Outcomes The relevant ILOs for this section are •​[ILO1] Use equations in implicit or parametric form including straight lines or conic sections to extract relevant information. •​[ILO2] Identify the appropriate partial fractions form and find the values of any coefficients for a rational function of a single variable. 1.1 Equations of lines and circles Learning Outcomes On completion of this subsection, students will be able to •​Define geometric properties of straight lines and circles algebraically. •​Solve geometric problems involving lines and circles. 1.1.1 Equation of a straight line An equation of the form equation (1.1.1) (1.1.1) ax+by=p for variables x and y , and constants a , b and p , represents a straight line in x – y space. The equation can be rearranged into other forms. The form equation (1.1.2) (1.1.2) y=mx+c is particularly useful. Here, m represents the gradient of the line and c represents the y -intercept, i.e. the point (0,c) where the line meets the y -axis (figure 1.1). Sketch of $y=mx+c$, showing that the y-coordinate of the line increases by $m$ for every distance 1 moved in the x-direction. Figure 1.1: Sketch of y=mx+c , showing that the y-coordinate of the line increases by m for every distance 1 moved in the x-direction. The animation in figure 1.2 (online version only) allows you to control the gradient and intercept of a straight line with sliders. Figure 1.2: Interactive plot of a straight line. Some useful properties of straight lines, as demonstrated in figure 1.3, are as follows (a)​Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient. For example, y=x/2+3 and y=x/2 are parallel. (b)​Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is -1 . For example, y=-3x+5 and y=x/3 are perpendicular. Note the exception is vertical lines, where the gradient is undefined. (c)​A horizontal line has equation y=c . (d)​A vertical line has equation x=d . (e)​Two lines cross at a point where they have the same value of y for a given value of x . Example 1.1.1 (DIY). Find the crossing point of the lines y=-\frac{1}{2}x+4,\qquad y=x+1. Solution Equate the two expressions for y : -\frac{1}{2}x+4=x+1. Rearranging gives 3=3x/2 , and hence x=2 . Substitution into the second equation gives y=2+1=3 . Therefore, (x,y)=(2,3). The straight-line distance between two points (x_{1},y_{1}) and (x_{2},y_{2}) is equation (1.1.4) (1.1.4) d=\sqrt{(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}}\,. Thus, the radius R=\sqrt{(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}} is the distance from any point (x,y) on the circle to its centre, which makes sense! (See figure 1.4). Refer to caption Figure 1.4: Sketch of a circle, with centre ( a , b ) and radius R , which is also the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle with side lengths x-a and y-b . Example 1.1.2 (Video). Find the centre and radius of the circle with equation x^{2}+4x+y^{2}-6y=3. Solution Complete the square for the quadratics in x and y : x^{2}+4x=(x+2)^{2}-4\,,\qquad y^{2}-6y=(y-3)^{2}-9. Substitute these expressions back into the equation for the circle: (x+2)^{2}-4+(y-3)^{2}-9=3\,, so (x+2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=16\,. Recall that the equation of a circle with centre (a,b) and radius R is (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2} . Therefore, a=-2\,,\qquad b=3,\qquad R=4. To find where a line and a circle cross, substitute the equation of the line, y=mx+c , into the equation of the circle, (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2} . This gives a quadratic equation for x , which may yield •​two solutions: the line and circle cross twice, •​one repeated solution: the line is tangent to the circle, •​no solutions: line and circle do not cross. These possibilities are shown in figure 1.5. Refer to caption (a) Two crossing points Refer to caption (b) One crossing point Refer to caption (c) No crossing points Figure 1.5: Three possibilities for the crossing points of a line and a circle. Example 1.1.3 (Lecture). Do the following line and circle cross? If so, at what point or points? y=x+1,\qquad(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=8. Solution Substitute the line equation into the circle and rearrange, equation equation Solve the resulting quadratic equation equation Next, substitute the solutions into the line equation to get y=\{0,4\}\,, respectively. Therefore, the line and circle cross at (-1,0) and (3,4) . At any point on a circle, the radius and tangent are perpendicular, as shown in figure 1.6(a). Useful definition: The perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB is a straight line that passes through the midpoint of AB and is perpendicular to it. A straight line segment connecting two points on a circle is a chord. Perpendicular bisector theorem: Given two points A and B , all points on the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB will be the same distance from A and B . Therefore, if A and B lie on a circle, the perpendicular bisector of the chord AB will pass through the centre, as shown in figure 1.6(b). Refer to caption (a) Tangent line Refer to caption (b) Perpendicular bisector Figure 1.6: Sketches of (a) the tangent to a circle, which is perpendicular to its radius and (b) the perpendicular bisector ( CD ) of two points on the circle ( A and B ), which passes through the circle’s centre E . Example 1.1.4 (Lecture). Find the equation of a circle with centre along the line y=2x-3 and which also passes through (1,6) and (5,2) . Solution Use the perpendicular bisector theorem. The gradient between the points is \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=-1\,. The midpoint is \left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}\right)=(3,4)\,. Therefore, the equation of the perpendicular bisector is y=x+1\,. The centre is the crossing point of the perpendicular bisector with y=2x-3 : (a,b)=(4,5)\,. To find R , substitute any point on the circle: R^{2}=(1-4)^{2}+(6-5)^{2}=10\,. Putting everything together gives (x-4)^{2}+(y-5)^{2}=10\,. \star Exam mistake of the week \star Trying to solve for three variables using only two equations. 25/26 Exam Q1(b): The (x,y) points A=(2,9) and B=(-5,2) lie on a circle with radius R and centre (a,b) . Given that the circle also touches, but does not cross, the x -axis find the two possible values of R and the corresponding values of (a,b) . Many students failed to use the information that the circle is tangent to the x -axis and attempted to solve by substituting the two given points into the circle equation, which is not sufficient to solve three unknowns ( a , b , and R ). Students attempted multiple ingenious approaches but this was ultimately time wasted. Note, this problem is Question 4 of Tutorial Sheet 1. Example 1.1.5 (Video). There are exactly two circles which touch, but do not cross, the x -axis and pass through A=(0,1) and B=(-2,5) . Find the centres, radii and hence the equations of these two circles. Solution The equation of a circle with centre (a,b) and radius R is given by equation (1.1.3). If the circle touches the x -axis, then R^{2}=b^{2} and so (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=b^{2}\,. or, expanding out, x^{2}-2ax+a^{2}+y^{2}-2by=0\,. Define y=mx+c as the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB . The gradient of the line AB is m_{AB}=(5-1)/(-2-0)=-2 and so m=1/2 . The midpoint of AB is (X,Y)=((0-2)/2,(1+5)/2)=(-1,3) , which lies on the bisector, therefore Y=mX+C and so c=Y-mX=3+1/2=7/2 Thus, the perpendicular bisector of AB is y=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{7}{2}\,, and so b=a/2+7/2 . Finally, any point on the circle, say A=(0,1) , must satisfy the equation x^{2}-2ax+a^{2}+y^{2}-2by=0 . Substituting in x=0 , y=1 gives a^{2}-a-6=0\,. Thus, a=3 or a=-2 , with corresponding values b=5 and b=5/2 respectively. Therefore, the two circles are given by the equations (x-3)^{2}+(y-5)^{2}=25\,, and (x+2)^{2}+\left(y-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{25}{4}. Sketch of the two circles that cross at $A=(0,1)$ and $B=(-2,5)$ and touch the $x$-axis. Recap Key points from section 1.1 •​Straight line equation: ax+by=p or y=mx+c . •​Equation of a circle: (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2} . •​Crossing point \rightarrow substitute the equation for the line into that of the circle. •​At a point on the circle, the radius and tangent are perpendicular. •​Given two points on the circle, an equation for a straight line passing through the circle’s centre can be found. 1.2 Explicit, implicit and parametric relations Learning Outcomes On completion of this subsection, students will be able to •​Recognise when relations between variables are in explicit, implicit or parametric form •​Reformulate explicit equations into parametric and implicit forms. 1.2.1 Implicit relations An explicit relation expresses the dependent variable (e.g. y ) as a function of the independent variable (e.g. x ), and so has the form y=f(x) . An example we have already met is the straight-line equation y=mx+c . Animplicit relation has the form equation (1.2.1) (1.2.1) f(x,y)=d\,, for some constant d . For a given value of x , there may be multiple y values that satisfy this (and vice versa). An example we have already met is the equation of a circle (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2}. In some cases, it is not possible to write a relation explicitly as y=f(x) . For example, 4x+8y+\sin(\pi x)+\cos(\pi y)=1 , which is plotted in figure 1.7, behaves like an explicit function, with one value of y for each x , however, we cannot reformulate it as an explicit function. Refer to caption Figure 1.7: A plot of the implicit function 4x+8y+\sin(\pi x)+\cos(\pi y)=1 . Example 1.2.1 (Video). An ellipse can be written in implicit form as \frac{x^{2}}{100}+\frac{y^{2}}{25}=1. For x=-10,-8,-6,0,6,8,10 , find the possible values of y and hence draw the ellipse. Solution Rearrange to get y in terms of x : \frac{y^{2}}{25}=1-\frac{x^{2}}{100} y=\pm 5\sqrt{1-\frac{x^{2}}{100}}=\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{100-x^{2}} Substitution gives {\begin{array}[]{|l|r|}\hline\cr x&y\\ \hline\cr-10&0\\ \hline\cr-8&\pm 3\\ \hline\cr-6&\pm 4\\ \hline\cr 0&\pm 5\\ \hline\cr 6&\pm 4\\ \hline\cr 8&\pm 3\\ \hline\cr 10&0\\ \hline\cr\end{array}} Plot of the ellipse using the caluclated points. 1.2.2 Parametric relations A parametric relation between x and y has the form equation (1.2.2) (1.2.2) x=f(t),\qquad y=g(t). So x and y are both functions of the parameter t . For example, the equation of a circle in parametric form is given by x=a+R\cos t,\qquad y=b+R\sin t, for 0\leq t<2\pi . The interactive animation in figure 1.8 demonstrates how parametric relations can be visualised by making the parameter t the coordinate of the third dimension. Figure 1.8: Interactive plot of the parametric curve x=\cos t , y=\sin t . The colour goes from white to red as t increases. Example 1.2.2 (DIY). Express the circle with centre at (2,3) and radius 4 in parametric form. Solution In parametric form x=a+R\cos t,\qquad y=b+R\sin t. For a=2 , b=3 , and R=4 , this gives x=2+4\cos t,\qquad y=3+4\sin t, for 0\leq t<2\pi . Given x=f(t) and y=g(t) , it may or may not be possible to express y directly as a function of x . For example, consider the parametric relation x=t^{2} , y=t^{4} . It can be written as y=x^{2} . However, for all values of t , x\geq 0 (see figure 1.9). Refer to caption Figure 1.9: Comparison of the function y=x^{2} and the parametric relation x=t^{2} , y=t^{4} . A general method to write parametric equations in explicit form is: •​rearrange the equation for the independent variable in terms of the parameter, i.e. rewrite x=f(t) into t=f^{-1}(x) ; •​substitute this into the equation for the dependent variable, i.e. replace t with f^{-1}(x) in y=g(t) . Note: t=f^{-1}(x) might not be unique, so be careful not to lose valid solutions! (E.g. x=t^{2} means t=\pm\sqrt{x} ). Example 1.2.3 (Lecture). Sodium oxide ( \mathrm{Na_{2}O} ) is placed in water producing sodium hydroxide: \mathrm{Na_{2}O+H_{2}O\longrightarrow 2NaOH}. The number of \mathrm{Na_{2}O} and \mathrm{NaOH} molecules in solution at time t\geq 0 is given by x=x_{0}e^{-\alpha t}\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x_{0}\left(1-e^{-\alpha t}\right) respectively, where x_{0} is the initial number of molecules of \mathrm{Na_{2}O} . Write y as a function of x , noting any restrictions on their values. Solution Find substitution for t in terms of x : e^{-\alpha t}=\frac{x}{x_{0}}. Substitute into equation for y : y=2(x_{0}-x). x is a decreasing function of t , since t\geq 0 , the minimum and maximum x values are 0<x\leq x_{0}. y is an increasing function of t , the minimum and maximum y values are 0\leq y<2x_{0}. The straight line and the circle can both be expressed in parametric and implicit form. Straight Line •​Implicit: ax+by=p . •​Parametric: x=bt , y=\frac{p}{b}-at . •​Explicit: y=-\frac{a}{b}x+\frac{p}{b}=mx+c . Circle •​Implicit: (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2} . •​Parametric: x=a+R\cos t , y=b+R\sin t . •​Explicit: y=b\pm\sqrt{R^{2}-(x-a)^{2}} . Recap Key points from section 1.2 •​An explicit relation expresses the dependent variable as a function of the independent variable (e.g. y=f(x) ). •​An implicit relation expresses the relationship between the variables via a function of both, (e.g. f(x,y)=0 ). •​A parametric relation expresses the variables as functions of a parameter (e.g. x=f(t) and y=g(t) ). 1.3 Partial fractions Learning Outcomes On completion of this subsection, students will be able to •​Simplify proper and improper compound fractions into partial fractions form 1.3.1 Partial fractions in general What do we mean by “partial fractions”? Consider the following sum of two fractions: \frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{3}{x-2}. We can put them over a common denominator to express as a single fraction (see figure 1.10): \frac{4x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)}. Partial fraction decomposition is about reversing this operation. This is often useful for differentiation and integration. Refer to caption Figure 1.10: Plots of the irreducible fractions \frac{1}{x+1} + and \frac{3}{x-2} and their sum, equivalent to \frac{4x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)} . Useful definitions: •​A rational fraction has a numerator and denominator that are both polynomials. •​The degree of a polynomial is the largest power in the polynomial, e.g. x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1=0 is degree 3. •​Defining d as the degree of the denominator and n as the degree of the numerator, then a proper fraction is a rational fraction where d>n . An improper fraction is a rational fraction where d\leq n . 1.3.2 Partial fractions for proper fractions Case 1: Linear function divided by factorising quadratic. A linear function divided by a factorising quadratic can be written in the form \frac{\text{linear}}{(x-a)(x-b)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}\,. To find A and B , first multiply both sides by the denominator (x-a)(x-b) to yield \text{linear}=A(x-b)+B(x-a). This equation must hold for all x . So, set x=a to find A (in terms of a , b , and the linear function) and set x=b to find B (in terms of a , b , and the linear function). Example 1.3.1 (Lecture). Express in partial fractions form \frac{x-4}{2x^{2}+5x-3}. Solution Factorise the denominator 2x^{2}+5x-3=(x+3)(2x-1). Write the form of the solution \frac{x-4}{(x+3)(2x-1)}=\frac{A}{x+3}+\frac{B}{2x-1}. Multiply through by the denominator x-4=A(2x-1)+B(x+3). Solve for A and B Substituting x=-3 gives -7=-7A , therefore A=1 Substituting x=1/2 gives -7/2=-7B/2 , therefore B=-1 and so \frac{x-4}{2x^{2}+5x-3}=\frac{1}{x+3}-\frac{1}{2x-1}. Case 2: Quadratic function divided by a factorising cubic. A quadratic function divided by a factorising cubic can be written in the form \frac{\text{quadratic}}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}+\frac{C}{% x-c}\,. To find A , B and C , multiply through by the denominator: \text{quadratic}=A(x-b)(x-c)+B(x-a)(x-c)+C(x-a)(x-b). Then set x=a to find A , x=b to find B , and x=c to find C . Case 1 and 2 generalise to any proper fraction with linear factors on the denominator: equation (1.3.1) (1.3.1) \frac{\text{degree }n-1\text{ polynomial}}{(x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})\cdots(x-x_{n})}=% \frac{A_{1}}{x-x_{1}}+\frac{A_{2}}{x-x_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{A_{n}}{x-x_{n}}. Example 1.3.2 (Video). Express in partial fractions form \frac{2x^{2}+8x+18}{x(x+2)(x-3)}. Solution The denominator contains 3 linear factors, so the correct form is \frac{2x^{2}+8x+18}{x(x+2)(x-3)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x+2}+\frac{C}{x-3}. Multiplying both sides by the denominator: 2x^{2}+8x+18=A(x+2)(x-3)+Bx(x-3)+Cx(x+2). This must hold for all x , so substitute x=0 to cancel B and C terms: 18=A(2)(-3)=-6A\qquad\therefore\;A=-3. Substitute x=-2 to cancel A and C terms: 8-16+18=B(-2)(-5)\qquad\therefore\;10B=10\qquad\therefore\;B=1. Substitute x=3 to cancel A and B terms: 18+24+18=C(3)(5)\qquad\therefore\;15C=60\qquad\therefore\;C=4. And so \frac{2x^{2}+8x+18}{x(x+2)(x-3)}=-\frac{3}{x}+\frac{1}{x+2}+\frac{4}{x-3}. Case 3: Repeated factor in the denominator. A repeated factor in the denominator results in two fractions, one with a square on the denominator, e.g. \frac{\text{quadratic}}{(x-a)^{2}(x-b)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^{2}}+% \frac{C}{x-b}\,. Multiplying both sides by the denominator: \text{quadratic}=A(x-a)(x-b)+B(x-b)+C(x-a)^{2}. Setting x=a and x=b only gives two of A , B , C . It is necessary to find the third by comparing coefficients of a power of x (e.g. comparing constants by setting x=0 ). This case also generalises to factors repeated n times, e.g. equation (1.3.2) (1.3.2) \frac{\text{degree }n\text{ polynomial}}{(x-a)(x-b)^{n}}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B% _{1}}{x-b}+\cdots+\frac{B_{n}}{(x-b)^{n}}. Example 1.3.3 (DIY). Write down the partial fractions form for \frac{x+9}{x(x^{2}-6x+9)}, but do not find the values of the coefficients. Solution Factorise the denominator: x^{2}-6x+9=(x-3)^{2}. Three terms required for x , x-3 , and (x-3)^{2} . Therefore, the partial fraction form is \frac{x+9}{x(x^{2}-6x+9)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-3}+\frac{C}{(x-3)^{2}}. Case 4: Irreducible quadratic in the denominator. An irreducible quadratic factor in the denominator results in a term of the form \frac{Ax+B}{\text{quadratic}} , e.g. \frac{\text{quadratic}}{(x^{2}+2x+9)(x-1)}=\frac{Ax+B}{x^{2}+2x+9}+\frac{C}{x-% 1}\,. Once again, it is necessary to use comparison of coefficients in order to find some of the values A , B , C etc. This rule generalises to irreducible polynomials of degree n , e.g. equation (1.3.3) (1.3.3) \frac{\text{degree }n\text{ polynomial}}{(x-a)(\text{irreducible degree }n% \text{ polynomial})}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+B_{1}x+B_{0}}{% \text{irreducible degree }n\text{ polynomial}}. Note: Here, we will take “irreducible” to mean that it cannot be factorised into integer roots. But, in general, the method works for all roots. E.g. In the following example, the quadratic has irrational solutions, and could be factorised using these, but you will not be asked to do this in this course. Example 1.3.4 (Video). Express in partial fractions form \frac{x^{2}}{(x-1)(x^{2}+3x-3)}. Solution The denominator cannot be factorised further, so the correct form is \frac{x^{2}}{(x-1)(x^{2}+3x-3)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^{2}+3x-3}. Multiplying both sides by the denominator and collecting powers of x : equation equation Compare coefficients of powers of x : x^{0}:\quad 0=-3A-C\qquad\therefore C=-3A, x:\quad 0=3A-B+C\qquad\therefore B=0, x^{2}:\quad 1=A+B\qquad A=1\qquad\therefore C=-3. And so \frac{x^{2}}{(x-1)(x^{2}+3x-3)}=\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{3}{x^{2}+3x-3}. 1.3.3 Partial fractions for improper fractions If a rational function has a denominator of degree n and a numerator of degree n+m , where m\geq 0 then the resultant partial fraction will include a polynomial of degree m , for example \displaystyle\frac{3x^{3}+x^{2}-x+6}{(x-2)(x+1)}=Ax+B+\frac{C}{x-2}+\frac{D}{x% +1} To find the coefficients, multiply both sides by the denominator and either substitute meaningful values of x or compare coefficients of powers of x . Example 1.3.5 (Lecture). Find the partial fractions form of \frac{3(x+1)^{2}}{x^{2}+x-2}. Solution Factorise the denominator: x^{2}+x-2=(x-1)(x+2). Identify correct form: \frac{3(x+1)^{2}}{(x-1)(x+2)}=A+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2}. Multiply through and solve for coefficients: equation equation Compare coefficients of powers of x : x^{2}:\quad A=3\,, x:\quad A+B+C=6\qquad\therefore B+C=3, x^{0}:\quad-2A+2B-C=3\qquad\therefore 2B-C=9\quad\therefore B=4\,,\,C=-1. Putting it all together \frac{3(x+1)^{2}}{x^{2}+x-2}=3+\frac{4}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+2}. Example 1.3.6 (Video). Find the partial fractions form for \frac{5x^{6}-50x^{5}+386x^{4}-1074x^{3}+644x^{2}+1174x-1354}{(x-2)^{2}(x^{2}-6% x+50)}, but do not find the values of the coefficients. Solution Check the degree of the numerator ( n ) and denominator ( d ): n=6\qquad\text{and}\qquad d=4\qquad\text{and so}\qquad n-d=2. Therefore the partial fractions form contains a quadratic. Check if the denominator factorises further It does not. Write the terms for the repeated root and the quadratic: Ax^{2}+Bx+C+\frac{D}{x-2}+\frac{E}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{Fx+G}{x^{2}-6x+50}. Recap Key points from section 1.3 •​Proper fractions ( d>n ): –​Linear factors in denominator \rightarrow\frac{A}{\text{linear}} –​Twice repeated linear factors \rightarrow\frac{A}{\text{linear}}+\frac{B}{\text{linear}^{2}} –​Quadratic factors in denominator \rightarrow\frac{Ax+B}{\text{quadratic}} •​Improper fractions ( d\leq n ): Add a polynomial of degree n-d •​General procedure: 1.​Factorise the denominator 2.​Classify the fraction and select the right form 3.​Multiply both sides by the denominator 4.​Compare coefficients (or choose values of x ) to solve for the constants Previous page Next page

This is a combination of two functions i.e. start with x , take the sine and then square it. x\quad\xrightarrow{\text{Take the sine}}\quad\sin x\quad\xrightarrow{\text{% Square it}}\quad(\sin x)^{2}. The inner function is g(x)=\sin x and the outer function is h(u)=u^{2} . The chain rule tells us how to differentiate a function of a function. Although written in implicit form, it can be differentiated. It is important to know which variable we are differentiating with respect to. In this case, we want to find {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x . Differentiate term-by-term with respect to x : •​The derivative of x^{2} is 2x •​Using the chain rule, the derivative of y^{2} is 2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x} •​The derivative of 25 is zero Therefore, we have 2x+2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=0. Which rearranges to \frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=-\frac{x}{y}. This is an example of implicit differentiation. The second derivative can also be found by repeating the process. Starting with x^{2}+y^{2}=25 and differentiating we get 2x+2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=0. •​Differentiating 2x gives 2 •​Using the product rule, differentiating 2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x} gives 2\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}\right)^{2}+2y\frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}} So, we find 2+2\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}\right)^{2}+2y\frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{% 2}}=0 or \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=-\frac{1+\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}% \right)^{2}}{y}. Substituting in the result from before ( {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x=-x/y ), this reduces to \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=-\frac{1}{y}-\frac{x^{2}}{y^{3}}. Alternatively, we could start with the result for {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x , i.e. \frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=-\frac{x}{y}. Use the quotient rule to differentiate, with u=-x and v=y , so u^{\prime}=-1 and v^{\prime}=y^{\prime} : \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=\frac{u^{\prime}v-v^{\prime}u}{v^{2}}=\frac{% -y+xy^{\prime}}{y^{2}}. Substituting in the previous result y^{\prime}=-x/y gives \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=\frac{-y-x^{2}/y}{y^{2}}=-\frac{1}{y}-\frac{% x^{2}}{y^{3}}, i.e. the same result as before. It can make derivatives simpler by taking advantage of the properties of logarithms, such as •​Transforming products into sums: \ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b •​Transforming powers into coefficients: \ln(x^{n})=n\ln x E.g. consider a function of the form y=f(x)g(x)h(x). On taking the logarithm of the absolute value of both sides, \ln|y|=\ln|fgh| =\ln|f|+\ln|g|+\ln|h|. Using implicit differentiation, the derivative of the left-hand side is \frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}x}(\ln|y|)=\frac{1}{y}\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}. Differentiating both sides and using this rule gives \frac{1}{y}\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}+\frac{g^{\prime}}{g}% +\frac{h^{\prime}}{h}. Therefore, using logarithmic differentiation y=f(x)g(x)h(x) gives \frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=y\left(\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}+\frac{g^{\prime}(x% )}{g(x)}+\frac{h^{\prime}(x)}{h(x)}\right). Given two vectors, \underline{\mathbf{a}} and \underline{\mathbf{b}} , the scalar product \underline{\mathbf{a}}\boldsymbol{\cdot}\underline{\mathbf{b}} is defined as equation (4.3.1) (4.3.1) \underline{\mathbf{a}}\boldsymbol{\cdot}\underline{\mathbf{b}}=\lvert% \underline{\mathbf{a}}\rvert\lvert\underline{\mathbf{b}}\rvert\cos\theta, where \theta is the angle between the vectors. Solution \overrightarrow{AB} and \overrightarrow{AC} lie in the plane, therefore \overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC} is perpendicular to the plane \overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ 0\\ 2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 5\\ 1\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 3\\ 3\end{pmatrix} equation equation equation Choose \underline{\mathbf{n}}=-\frac{1}{6}(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{% AC})=\underline{\mathbf{i}}+2\underline{\mathbf{j}}-3\underline{\mathbf{k}} and \underline{\mathbf{a}}=2\underline{\mathbf{j}}-2\underline{\mathbf{k}} then \underline{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\underline{\mathbf{n}}=4+6=10 and so the equation of the plane is \underline{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ -3\end{pmatrix}=10 Example 4.5.4 (Video). Find where the line \underline{\mathbf{r}}_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix} intersects the plane \underline{\mathbf{r}}\boldsymbol{\cdot}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=5. Solution Substitute \underline{\mathbf{r}}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix} into the equation for the plane \begin{pmatrix}1\\ -2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=5 and so \qquad 1+2\lambda=5 which gives \lambda=2 .
